archetype.name: Pocket Passer (aggressive)
archetype.definition: A statue-in-the-pocket timing thrower who wins with anticipation over the middle and outside the numbers, takes almost no sacks, and has always accepted a high interception rate as the cost of throwing into tight windows.

report.headline: Volume and intermediate precision are carrying him; the deep ball hasn't shown up yet.
report.take:
Stafford at 38 is the same quarterback the career lines describe. He stands in, gets the ball out on time, rarely takes a sack, and throws into windows other passers pass up. His interception ranks have sat in the bottom third almost every season since 2009. What's new in 2026 is how heavily the Rams lean on him. They pass four points over expectation (5th in the league), and he has thrown 55, 51 and 54 times in the last three games. That volume is why he leads the position in passing yards while sitting 16th in EPA per dropback. The yardage is real, but it reflects workload more than peak efficiency.

The engine is the 10-19 yard band. On 52 intermediate throws he's at +0.366 EPA with a 55.8% success rate, and short passing (+0.171 on 114 attempts) keeps the chains moving. The no-huddle numbers (+0.40 EPA, 13.1 CPOE on 34 plays) suggest he's sharpest when he's running the operation at tempo. Protection has been excellent: pressured on 13.5% of dropbacks (5th) and sacked on 3.1% (4th). That is partly the line and partly a 2.76-second clock he has run for years.

The weak spot is deep. He has 7 completions on 24 throws of 20+ air yards, three interceptions and negative EPA. That accounts for half his picks on about a tenth of his attempts. It doesn't fit last season, when he led the league with 46 TDs at a 9.2 aDOT. Twenty-four throws is a small sample, so read it more as cold variance plus some timing still being worked out than as an arm that has gone. His game-to-game results also follow the opponent closely. Against SF and Denver (4th and 7th in defensive EPA today) he produced -5.6 and -0.7 passing EPA. Against the Giants and Bills (22nd and 30th) he produced +18.6 and +18.5. Third down (-0.088 EPA) and the right side of the field (4 of his 6 INTs) are where the mistakes cluster.

Going forward, the floor is set by volume and protection, and the ceiling depends on the opponent. Arizona is close to the friendliest pass defense on paper he'll see all year.

strengths.title: Intermediate-window precision
strengths.body: The 10-19 yard throws are where his anticipation shows. He completes them at a rate that produces big EPA even with a slightly negative CPOE, because each completion moves the ball so far. This is the same skill set that drove his 2025 season, so it should hold up.

strengths.title: Clean pocket, almost no sacks
strengths.body: He's pressured less than almost any qualifier and turns little of that pressure into sacks. That keeps drives alive even when the deep shots miss. His pressure-to-sack rate has improved three years running (24.6% in 2024, 19.7% in 2025), so this looks structural.

strengths.title: Volume-driven yardage floor
strengths.body: McVay is putting the game on him: three straight games of 51+ attempts in a pass-heavy scheme. Even with middling efficiency, that keeps him at the top of the position in yards. The role, not the hot streak, is what sustains it.

concerns.title: Deep ball misfiring
concerns.body: He is 7-of-24 on throws of 20+ air yards with three interceptions. That is the main drag on his EPA and his interception rate. Last season's league-leading TD total argues this is a cold patch, but he has already pulled back his intended air yards (6.7 against Buffalo), and that could cap his ceiling if it continues.

concerns.title: Interceptions, as always
concerns.body: His 2.8% interception rate ranks 33rd, and he has thrown a pick in four of five games. This is partly the cost of his aggressiveness and is consistent with his whole career, so expect it to ease toward his recent norm rather than disappear. The right side of the field and third down are where the mistakes cluster.

concerns.title: Good defenses shut him down
concerns.body: Against the two top-seven defenses he has faced, he produced negative passing EPA. In Week 1 he was pressured on 28% of dropbacks, and in Week 3 he was sacked four times. The splits are flattered by Buffalo and New York, so keep his opponent in mind when judging any single week.

trend.note: His results have swung with the opponent: -5.6, +18.6, -0.7, +1.1 and +18.5 passing EPA. The two big games came against bottom-ten defenses and the two worst against top-seven units. He has climbed out of a rough opener, with two strong games in the last three.

nextGame.headline: Arizona's sieve of a secondary meets a 50-attempt passer
nextGame.body:
Arizona ranks 31st in defensive pass EPA, 32nd in explosive pass rate allowed, and near the bottom on both deep and short throws. That is the profile of the Giants and Bills defenses he carved up, not the SF or Denver defenses that stymied him. Arizona has been especially generous to WR1s (0.87 EPA per target, worst in the league) and tight ends. That suits a passing tree where Davante Adams and Tyler Higbee have been his most efficient targets. The one real strength of this defense is its pass rush: a 7% sack rate ranks 10th, so the pocket may be a bit busier than usual. A deep ball that has been misfiring also gets its best chance to correct here.

Availability tilts further his way. Arizona is without safety Andrew Wingard (76% of snaps), and backup safety Wydett Williams Jr. is questionable with a concussion, leaving the back end thin against intermediate and deep throws. On the other side, Arizona's offense has lost left tackle Paris Johnson Jr. and guard Isaiah Adams to IR. That makes a lopsided game more plausible, and that is the main risk to his volume: a 13.5-point spread means a fourth quarter he may not need. For the Rams, Stafford is healthy, and with Terrance Ferguson on IR until November, Higbee keeps the tight end targets against a defense that leaks to the position.

keyMatchups.title: Adams vs. the league's worst WR1 defense
keyMatchups.body: Adams has been his most efficient high-volume target, and Arizona has allowed more EPA per WR1 target than anyone. With a safety out, the routes outside the numbers where Stafford does his best work should be open.

keyMatchups.title: Higbee against a TE-friendly defense
keyMatchups.body: Arizona allows tight ends 5.4 PPR above their averages (30th) and sees an above-league share of targets go to the position. Higbee has been Stafford's other +0.4 EPA target, and the injuries at TE leave him as the only real option there.

keyMatchups.title: Blowout script vs. his volume
keyMatchups.body: A double-digit lead could cut his attempts, though he has still been efficient when ahead by 9+ (+0.239 EPA), and in the Week 2 blowout of New York he still threw for 327. Arizona's top-ten sack rate is the other threat to his drives.

nextGame.watch: Whether he takes and hits deep shots against a short-handed Arizona secondary that ranks 30th against deep passes. That is the test of whether his deep struggles are noise.

restOfSeason.body:
The volume should stay. McVay's pass-heavy tilt and Stafford's protection give him a floor of roughly 270-300 yards a week against average defenses. Yardage may dip slightly from the current 314-a-game pace as game scripts even out. His deep accuracy should regress upward toward his 2025 form, which would lift both his TD rate (4.2% now, well below last season) and his EPA. His interception rate should ease but not vanish; it never has in his career. The third-down slump and right-side split rest on small samples and are likely to improve.

The swing is opponent quality. Against top-ten defenses he has looked like a league-average passer, and against weak ones like a top-five passer. With Ferguson back in November, the tight end room gets deeper. The main downside risk is a 38-year-old carrying a 50-attempt workload over a full season.

bets.reason: Arizona allows 3 TDs a game to quarterbacks (30th) and ranks 31st in pass EPA, with a starting safety out. Stafford has 7 TDs on 28 red-zone throws, and his two games against bottom-ten defenses produced 4 and 3 TDs.

Arizona is last in explosive pass rate allowed and 30th against deep throws, and the Rams pass well above expectation. A blowout could trim his volume, but he threw for 327 in the 28-6 win over New York, so a lead hasn't stopped the passing.

He has thrown a pick in four of five games with a 2.8% INT rate, and his career rates say this is who he is. The edge is modest because Arizona's thin secondary may produce more completions than takeaways.

confidence.note: Five games, with results heavily tied to opponent quality, but a long career profile anchors the read.
